::: {.callout-note title="Before you start"}
Read the [micelle tutorial](micelle.qmd) for distributed surface links and
[Reuse a composite component](nested-structures.qmd) for graph instances.
This page combines those two operations; no fitting knowledge is needed yet.
:::

We will build and evaluate one four-cylinder arm, inspect it in 3D, then
attach copies to a spherical core. The result is a reusable corona topology.
The next page supplies experimental data and fits its dimensions.

## Set up the environment

Use the environment from the prerequisites with `pyseb[visualization]`, NumPy,
and Jupyter installed. Run this page from `docs/tutorials` in a repository
checkout; it writes downloadable scenes under `generated/f127-corona`.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pyseb
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve().parents[1]
SCENE_DIR = Path("generated/f127-corona").resolve()
SCENE_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
q = np.geomspace(1e-3, 0.5, 100)


def scene_link(path, text):
    relative = path.relative_to(ROOT / "docs/tutorials").as_posix()
    display(Markdown(f"[{text}]({relative})"))
```

## 1. Start with one segment

A `World` holds our subunits and connections. `Add` creates the first cylinder
and returns the graph containing it. The name `segment0` identifies this
instance; the tag `segment` shares its dimensions with the segments we add next.

```{python}
world = pyseb.World("F127Tutorial")
chain = world.Add("SolidCylinder", "segment0", "segment")
```

## 2. Connect four segments into one arm

`Link` adds another cylinder and joins its `bottom` reference to the previous
cylinder's `top`. Repeating that step makes a chain. Every cylinder has the same
`segment` tag, so we fit one segment size for the whole arm.

```{python}
for index in range(1, 4):
    world.Link(
        "SolidCylinder",
        f"segment{index}.bottom",
        f"segment{index-1}.top",
        "segment",
    )

world.Add(chain, "arm")
```

`world.Add(chain, "arm")` names the complete connected structure. We can now
calculate its scattering or export it as one reusable object.

Before fitting anything, evaluate the connected arm directly with pySEB.
The shared tag gives us `R_segment`, `L_segment`, and `beta_segment`.
`EvaluateFormFactor` returns the normalized form factor on our chosen
q grid, including interference between the four linked cylinders.

```{python}
parameters = {"R_segment": 5., "L_segment": 30., "beta_segment": 1.}
arm_form_factor = np.asarray(
    world.EvaluateFormFactor("arm", parameters, q.tolist())
)
assert arm_form_factor.shape == q.shape

plt.loglog(q, arm_form_factor)
plt.xlabel(r"$q$ [Å$^{-1}$]")
plt.ylabel(r"$F(q)$")
plt.show()
```

## 3. See what we built

Use the same cylinder dimensions to display the **actual pySEB graph**
with `pyseb.visualize`. We also save an OpenUSD scene for download.
Drag to rotate and scroll to zoom.

```{python}
options = pyseb.USDExportOptions(pyseb.LengthUnit.Angstrom)
options.seed = 127
options.surface_samples = 16
options.curve_samples = 64
options.layout_mode = pyseb.LayoutMode.Readable
options.orientation_trials = 8
options.relaxation_sweeps = 1

arm_path = SCENE_DIR / "four-cylinder-arm.usda"
world.export_usd("arm", str(arm_path), parameters, options)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
_ = pyseb.visualize(world, "arm", parameters, options, height=420, layouts=["random", "readable"])
scene_link(arm_path, "Download the OpenUSD arm")
```

## 4. Attach copies of the arm to a core

Add a sphere for the core. A concentric zero-contrast sphere supplies surface
attachment points at an adjustable distance from the core centre; it does
not contribute scattering.

```{python}
micelle = world.Add("SolidSphere", "core")
world.Link("SolidSphere", "anchor.center", "core.center")
```

Reuse the **same chain graph** for each arm. `arm0`, `arm1`, and the other names
identify separate copies; `segment0.bottom` identifies the root of each copy.
Each `surface#p...` is an independently distributed attachment point.

```{python}
for index in range(96):
    world.Link(
        chain,
        f"arm{index}:segment0.bottom",
        f"anchor.surface#p{index}",
    )

world.Add(micelle, "micelle")
```

This creates a sphere with 96 four-cylinder arms. In the [next page’s fit](fit-f127-data.qmd), the average
arm count follows the core volume rather than being fixed at 96. The final
scene uses the nearest integer count for the fitted mean core size.
